title: Who Decided You Weren’t High Potential?
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez critiques high-potential (HiPo) programs without rejecting intentional talent development. Her central claim is that these programs conflate current performance with future potential and rely on manager nominations and gut instinct, so they reward visibility, charisma and familiarity and reproduce the nominators' own backgrounds. She sees two harms: designated high potentials often lack fundamentals like emotional intelligence and developing others, while the much larger group left off the list disengages and then fulfils the prophecy that they had little potential. Drawing on Dweck's growth mindset and Google's Project Oxygen, she argues that leadership capability is a set of learnable behaviours, so potential is built rather than found. She closes with an audit of who nominates, what happens to those excluded, and whether the definition of potential matches the organization's future.
points: Only one in four leaders call their HiPo strategy effective, partly because programs confuse current performance with future potential.
Nomination by managers and gut instinct measures visibility and familiarity, and so replicates existing demographic patterns.
Programs harm twice: selected people may lack core leadership skills, and excluded people receive fewer opportunities and fulfil a low prediction.
Potential is built, not found; Project Oxygen shows effective behaviours can be identified and taught to a wide range of people.
A quick audit of nominators, criteria, and the experience of those left off the list exposes where a program is failing.
quotes: Still, despite all of that investment, only one in four people leaders describe their organization’s HiPo strategy as actually effective.

many programs have a persistent tendency to reward charisma, confidence, and strong performance over the aptitudes that actually predict whether someone will be effective in a more complex, more senior role—things like learning agility, emotional intelligence, and the capacity to develop and bring out the best in other humans. In other words, we focus on the stuff that’s most visible, rather than the stuff that’s really needed for what comes next.

When we ask managers to nominate people “with potential” without providing clear, defined criteria for what we mean, we shouldn’t be surprised when the resulting list reflects the backgrounds, identities, and personality preferences of the people doing the nominating. And so the status quo remains.

What follows here is often a sort of self-fulfilling prophecy wherein the employees who aren’t labeled as high potential receive fewer supports and opportunities. In the end, the organization gets back exactly what it implicitly predicted and then interprets this outcome as confirmation that the process they underwent for selection is viable.

The underlying logic in naming this here is that leadership capability isn’t a genetic trait exhibited exclusively within a select cohort. Instead, it’s a set of learnable behaviors that a much wider range of people can develop when given support and opportunity. In other words, high potential is built.

Who is doing the nominating of high potentials, and what criteria are they using? If your selection process runs primarily through manager nominations without a validated framework underneath it, you’re measuring visibility and familiarity more than you’re measuring potential.
